draft.title: Social, moral and ethical positions
card: A literary text often takes a position on what is right, fair or just. The position may be stated outright, or it may be shown through events and characters.
Readers can find a position by asking what the text treats as admirable or shameful, and who it asks the audience to sympathise with.
A reader does not simply accept the position. They evaluate it: they ask what evidence in the text supports it, whose view is left out, and whether it seems fair.
Evaluating a position is not the same as agreeing or disagreeing with it. A reader can see that a text argues well for a view and still question that view.
draft.remember: Find the position the text takes, then test it against the text instead of accepting it.

a.q: In a short story, a shopkeeper is rewarded for refusing to cheat a customer, while a rival who cheats is shunned. What is the story doing?
opts: Taking a moral position that honesty is right
Proving that all shopkeepers are honest
Giving a neutral report of how shops run
Showing that rewards are always fair
a.why: The story treats honesty as admirable and cheating as shameful, which is a moral position. It does not prove anything about all shopkeepers, and it is not neutral because it rewards one choice and punishes the other.
a.clue: Notice who is rewarded and who is shunned.

b.q: A novel shows a town leader forcing a family from their home and invites readers to admire him as strong. Which response best evaluates the text's position?
opts: Ask whether the text shows the family's view fairly
Accept that strong leaders are always right
Reject the novel because it shows an unfair act
Say the position cannot be discussed at all
b.why: Evaluating means testing the position against the text, such as whose view is shown or left out. Accepting it simply follows the text, and rejecting the novel because of the event is not evaluation, since a text can show an unfair act without endorsing it.
b.clue: Evaluating means testing the text's view, not just accepting or refusing it.

a.best: Taking a moral position that honesty is right

b.best: Ask whether the text shows the family's view fairly

problems.detail: Why (b) says rejecting is wrong 'since a text can show an unfair act without endorsing it'. But the stem says this novel invites readers to admire the leader, so it does endorse the act. The real reason rejecting falls short is that it refuses the position without testing it against the text.
Two wrong options rely on absolutes ('always fair', 'all shopkeepers'). A student can rule them out by the extreme wording alone, without knowing the idea.

Wrong option 'Accept that strong leaders are always right' uses 'always', so it is easy to eliminate on wording alone. The clue also rules out both accepting and refusing, which leaves the answer almost given away.

check.summary: Both answers are correct. Why (b) gives a reason that clashes with its own stem, since the novel does endorse the leader. Some wrong options use absolutes ('always', 'all') that make them easy to rule out.

a.q: In a short story, a shopkeeper is rewarded for refusing to cheat a customer, while a rival who cheats is shunned. What is the story doing?
opts: Treating honesty as right and cheating as shameful
Treating cheating as clever and honesty as foolish
Reporting events without judging either shopkeeper
Judging the customer for trusting the shopkeeper
a.why: The story rewards the honest shopkeeper and shuns the cheat, so it treats honesty as admirable and cheating as shameful. It is not neutral: choosing who is rewarded and who is shunned is how a text shows its position through events.
a.clue: Notice who is rewarded and who is shunned.

b.q: A novel shows a town leader forcing a family from their home and invites readers to admire him as strong. Which response best evaluates the text's position?
opts: Test whether the text gives the family's side fairly
Agree that the leader is strong, as the text suggests
Reject the novel because the leader acts unfairly
Identify the leader as the novel's main character
b.why: Evaluating means testing the position against the text, such as asking whether the family's view is shown or left out. Rejecting the novel is disagreement, not evaluation: it refuses the position without testing it against the text. Agreeing simply accepts the position the text offers.
b.clue: Think about which characters the novel lets readers hear from.
